parts.title: The night the ground shook
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
I was twelve when I felt my first big earthquake. We were living in a small town in Chile, near the mountains, and it was a quiet Sunday evening. My father was cooking, my mother was reading, and my brother and I were playing a card game on the floor.

Suddenly, the lights began to shake and a glass fell off the table. At first, I thought that a lorry was passing in the street, but the noise became louder and louder. My mother shouted, "Under the table, now!" and we all crawled under it. The shaking lasted for almost a minute, but it felt like an hour.

When it was over, we went into the street with our neighbours. Nobody in our building was hurt, although the road in front of us had a long crack, and some old walls had fallen down. Everyone was talking at the same time, and a few children were crying.

Since that night, I have always known where to take cover, and I keep a torch next to my bed. My mother says that the best thing about the earthquake was that we spent the whole evening together, talking and laughing in the street.

questions.prompt: What was the family doing when the earthquake began?
options: They were sleeping in their beds
They were eating a late dinner
They were watching the news on television
They were busy with quiet activities
questions.explanation: The father was cooking, the mother was reading, and the children played cards.

questions.prompt: What did the writer think the noise was at first?
options: A lorry passing in the street
A storm coming from the hills
questions.explanation: She thought that a lorry was passing in the street.

questions.prompt: What did the family do when the shaking started?
options: They ran outside to the street
They called their neighbours for help
They hid under the dining table
They ran into the garden at once
questions.explanation: They crawled under the table when her mother shouted.

questions.prompt: What was the situation after the earthquake?
options: The neighbours had all left town
A long crack ran along the road
Many walls in the building fell
Some people in the building were hurt
questions.explanation: The road in front of them had a long crack and nobody was hurt.

questions.prompt: What does the writer's mother say was good about that night?
options: The streets were empty and calm
Nobody needed to go to work
The earthquake lasted only a minute
They were together for the evening
questions.explanation: She says they spent the whole evening together, talking and laughing.

parts.title: How does a volcano work?
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
A volcano is a hole in the Earth's surface through which hot, melted rock can escape. [1] Deep underground, the rock is so hot that it turns into a thick liquid called magma.

Magma is lighter than the rock around it, so it slowly rises. [2] When it reaches the surface, we call it lava, and it can be hotter than a thousand degrees.

Not all eruptions are the same. Some volcanoes send out a slow river of lava that moves only a few metres an hour. [3] Others explode with great force and throw ash and stones high into the sky.

Scientists watch many volcanoes day and night. [4] If the ground begins to shake, they know that an eruption may be near and can warn the people.

Although volcanoes can be dangerous, they also bring good things. [5] This is why many farmers choose to grow their crops on the slopes of old volcanoes.
sentences: The soil formed from old ash is rich and full of minerals.
Fortunately, they are far from any town.
Many of these are in countries around the Pacific Ocean.
It collects in a large space under the mountain and pushes upwards.
Sometimes it finds a crack and bursts out into the air.
The fastest of these can destroy houses and roads in a short time.
One of the biggest eruptions in history happened in Indonesia in 1815.
They use special instruments to measure small movements of the ground.

gaps.explanation: Many volcanoes are around the Pacific Ocean, and the next sentence explains why the rock deep underground is so hot.
Magma that rises collects in a space under the mountain and pushes upwards, then bursts out.
Slow rivers are compared with the fastest ones, which can destroy houses and roads.
Scientists use special instruments to measure small movements, and the next sentence says the ground may shake.
The rich soil from old ash is a good thing that explains why farmers choose these slopes.

parts.title: Living near a volcano
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Millions of people live close to active volcanoes, and many of them are not afraid. They know that an eruption is rare, and they [1] taught what to do if one begins. In some towns, families keep a bag with food, water and a torch [2] the front door. Schools practise the way out of the building several times a year, [3] the children know what to do. When the volcano gets noisy, scientists tell the radio, [4] the whole town can hear it. Most people say that the good things are more important than the dangers: the soil is rich, the views are wonderful, and visitors come from all [5] the world. It is a life that is [6] always easy, but many families would never move away.

gaps.explanation: They are taught: passive form with a plural subject.
A bag by the front door means next to it.
So that the children know: purpose clause.
So the whole town can hear: result of telling the radio.
From all over the world means from every part.
It is not always easy: negative form of the verb.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Hi, Anand, it’s Anaya. About tomorrow’s trip to the volcano museum. I said a quarter to six when we spoke yesterday, but I’ve checked the bus, and it leaves from the station at a quarter past six, so that’s far too late for the first tour. I thought of six o’clock too, but then you’d have to run, and the doors open at six. The best plan is half an hour before that. So let’s meet in front of the station at the time when the sky is just getting light. Bring a warm jacket. See you there!

question.explanation: A quarter to six was her first idea and six is when the doors open; the plan is half an hour before that, so they meet at half past five.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Arjun, did you feel the earthquake this morning? It was on the news, and my cups were shaking.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Honestly, I slept through the whole thing. My brother says that he ran out of the house in his pyjamas, and the neighbours were shouting in the street. They said there was a terrible noise, like a lorry.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I heard it too. It was like thunder.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Well, I missed it. I woke up at eight, had breakfast, and only read about it on my phone. I feel a bit silly.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You’re lucky. I couldn’t sleep afterwards.

question.prompt: What does the man say about the earthquake?
options: He ran out of the house
He heard a very loud noise
question.explanation: Others heard a noise and his brother ran out, but he slept and felt nothing.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Good morning, and welcome to the Volcano Visitor Centre. Many of you ask me when the volcano last erupted. Some people believe it was last summer, because there was smoke over the top for a week, but that was only steam from the hot ground. A more recent event happened ten years ago, when a small crack opened on the side, and the village was quiet for a few days. But the last real eruption, with fire and ash, was about a hundred years ago. My grandmother told me stories about it. So nothing big has happened in a long time, and you are safe on our walk.

question.prompt: When did the volcano last erupt?
question.explanation: Smoke last summer was only steam, and the crack ten years ago was small; the last real eruption was about a hundred years ago.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Why do you keep a torch next to your bed, Armand? Do you read at night?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: A friend gave it to me as a present, but that isn’t the reason, and I read with my phone. It’s there for the power cuts.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Do you have a lot of them?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: In winter, quite often. The wind knocks down the lines, and the whole street goes dark. Once I fell over the cat trying to find the door. Now I can find my way without hurting myself.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s a sensible idea. I should do the same.

question.prompt: Why is the torch next to the bed?
options: It is a present from his friend
It is for when the lights go out
It helps him to read at night
question.explanation: It was a present and he reads on his phone; he keeps it for when the lights go out in a power cut.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Hi, Asha, it’s Aneurin. I wanted to ask about the film you saw. Did you like it? My friend said the plot was ridiculous, and a lot of people left halfway because it was so slow.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Hi, Aneurin. Funny that you call. I know what they mean, and I admit I looked at my watch twice in the middle, but I wasn’t angry or bored. I stayed, and when the main character said goodbye to her dog at the end, I started to cry. The last scene was so sad that I couldn’t speak in the car. You should see it, but bring tissues.

question.prompt: How did the woman feel at the end of the film?
question.explanation: The plot was slow, and she looked at her watch, but she was not angry or bored; the last scene made her cry.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Welcome to the museum, everyone. Before you start, a few words about our rock collection, which many of you come to see. Please don’t look for it near the entrance, next to the ticket desk. That’s where we used to keep it, but we got tired of children touching things. A few people also ask about the shelf near the door, but that has our postcards. The rocks, the best ones from the last eruption, are now protected inside a glass case in the first room, just after the stairs. You can look as long as you like, but please don’t lean on it.

options: On the shelf near the door
question.explanation: The old place was next to the ticket desk and the shelf near the door has postcards; the rocks are in a glass case in the first room.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I saw a house for sale at the foot of the mountain, Anaya. It’s cheap and the garden is huge. Would you live there?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: No way. I don’t mind the heat, it’s the opposite of a problem. And the price isn’t the point, I’d buy it today if I could.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So what’s wrong with it?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: The ash. Every time the mountain wakes up, ash covers everything and you can’t breathe. My cousin lives in one of those villages, and she wears a mask at home. I’d be afraid all the time.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I didn’t think about that.

question.prompt: Why doesn't the woman want to live near a volcano?
options: She hates the smell of smoke
question.explanation: She says the heat does not bother her and the price is good; she would be afraid of the ash falling from the volcano.

parts.title: Understanding the main idea
parts.instructions: Listen to six short conversations and choose the best answer.

turns.speaker: f

turns.speaker: m

options: It is too difficult for his class
It is interesting for the students

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’ve found a flat next to the mountain, Asha. I’m going to take it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Is it for the view? It’s beautiful, I admit.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: The view is good, of course, but it isn’t the main reason. It’s ten minutes from my office, but I could get that anywhere in the town. What I like is the rent. It’s half the price of my last flat, and I can finally save money.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I understand, but isn’t it dangerous?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’ll worry about that later.

question.prompt: Why does Armand want the flat?
question.explanation: She mentions the view and he admits the walk to work could be found anywhere, but the main reason is that the rent is half the price.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Did you hear about the new visitor centre near the volcano, Arjun? Some people are angry about it.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I know. They say it will spoil the view of the mountain, and I understand that, it is a lovely place. And the town council will pay a lot of money for it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: So are you against it?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: No, I’m in favour. Honestly, my cousins have no work, and the centre will need guides, cooks and cleaners. That’s much more important than a view. I think the town needs it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Maybe you’re right.

question.prompt: What does Arjun think of the plan for a new visitor centre?
options: It will bring jobs to the town
question.explanation: He accepts that the building may spoil the view and cost money, but he supports it because it will give work to people in the town.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Good morning, can I help you?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I hope so. I want to know if you are open on Sundays. I work all week and I can only come at the weekend.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: We close on Saturday at one, I’m afraid, and we don’t open on Sundays.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s a pity. I wanted to find a book about volcanoes, but I can look at the website. And I don’t have anything to return, I gave my books back last week.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You can also use the machine outside at night.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Good idea, thanks.

question.prompt: Why does Aragorn visit the library?
options: To look for a book on volcanoes
To ask when it opens on Sundays
question.explanation: He asks about Sunday hours; he can look for the volcano book online and has nothing to return.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: So you’re a guide on the volcano, Asha. Isn’t that dangerous?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Not really. We follow safe paths, and there are rules. People think I must earn very little, but the money is fair.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I’m sure it is. I was going to say that you’re brave, but I think it’s more than that. You’re outside every day, with the sky and the mountain, and you meet people from everywhere. I’m stuck in an office.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Come with me one day.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I’d love to. I’d even do it for free.

question.prompt: What does Aneurin think about Asha's job?
options: He would like to try it
question.explanation: He does not worry about danger or pay; he says it is better than his office and he wants to do it.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: My flight has been cancelled because of the ash cloud, Anaya. I don’t know what to do. I could buy a new ticket.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Don’t. The airline has to pay for your hotel and your meals when the flight is cancelled, so you shouldn’t spend any money.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: What about taking the train home? I’d go tonight.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It’s twelve hours, and you’ll be exhausted. Go to the desk and tell them you need a room. They’ll move you to the next flight.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: You’re right. I’ll go there now.

question.prompt: What does Anaya advise Anand to do?
options: Ask the airline for a hotel
question.explanation: A new ticket is not needed because the airline pays, and the train is too long; she tells him to ask the airline for a hotel.

parts.title: A talk about Mount Vesuvius
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: livia
turns.text: Hello, everyone. Today, I would like to talk about Mount Vesuvius, a famous volcano. Some visitors think that it is in Greece, but it is in the south of Italy, close to the city of Naples. You can see it from the bay, and many photographers love it. The most famous eruption happened in the year seventy-nine. There was another big one in sixteen thirty-one, but seventy-nine is the one that everybody remembers. On that day, two towns near the mountain, Pompeii and Herculaneum, were buried. You may think that rivers of lava killed the people, but in fact, it was the ash that covered the streets and the houses. It fell for hours, and it was hot, so the people could not escape. For many centuries the towns stayed under the ground. Workers started to dig in the eighteenth century, a long time after the eruption. In the nineteenth century, a lot more work was done, and the first big museum opened, but it was in the seventeen hundreds that the digging began. It took a long time to uncover the streets. Today you can walk in them. One of the most interesting places is an old bakery. You can see the oven, and there are even loaves of bread inside. People often ask about the shops, but the bakery is the one with the bread, and it is the most photographed place. Finally, you may ask about the volcano today. It has not been quiet all the time. There was an eruption in nineteen hundred and six, which damaged villages. The last eruption was in nineteen forty-four. Since then, it has been calm, but scientists watch it carefully, day and night. Thank you for listening.

gaps.prompt: The volcano is in the south of ___, close to Naples
gaps.explanation: Some visitors think it is in Greece, but it is in southern Italy.

gaps.prompt: The eruption that everybody remembers happened in the year ___
gaps.explanation: Another eruption was in sixteen thirty-one, but the one that everybody remembers was in seventy-nine.

gaps.prompt: What killed the people was not lava but the ___ that fell for hours
gaps.explanation: The speaker says that it was the ash that covered the streets and the houses.

gaps.prompt: The digging began in the ___ century
gaps.explanation: The first museum opened in the nineteenth century, but digging started in the eighteenth.

gaps.prompt: Tourists can see loaves of bread in an old ___
gaps.explanation: The old bakery has an oven with loaves of bread inside.

gaps.prompt: There has been no eruption since ___
gaps.explanation: There was an eruption in nineteen hundred and six, but the last one was in nineteen forty-four.

parts.title: An interview with a volcano scientist
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Andile, you study volcanoes for a living. When did you first get interested?

turns.speaker: s
turns.text: I’d like to say it was a family holiday, but we never went near one, and I didn’t read about lava in a book either. It was a short video at school. The teacher showed it on a rainy Monday, and I couldn’t stop looking at the glowing rivers. I remember that I asked her if I could watch it again.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you do on a normal day?

turns.speaker: s
turns.text: People imagine I run up mountains every day, but most days I sit at a desk. I’m not a writer, and I don’t teach at a university, at least not yet. I look at numbers from machines that we place on the volcano, and they tell us how the ground moves and how hot it is.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How do you stay safe near the crater?

turns.speaker: s
turns.text: First of all, we wear a helmet and a mask, because the gas can hurt your lungs. That’s the most important rule. We don’t go only in the cold, the weather doesn’t change the danger, and we carry little food because it’s heavy. But we always check the wind before we start to walk.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Tell me about the most exciting moment in your career.

turns.speaker: s
turns.text: It wasn’t a prize, although I was proud when I won one, and I haven’t met any famous scientist. It was one night when I saw red lava coming out of the ground. I was a long way away, but the colour was so strong that I forgot to take pictures. I just stood there and smiled. I was amazed.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Can scientists tell when a volcano is going to erupt?

turns.speaker: s
turns.text: We can’t say the exact day, that’s impossible, and nobody can stop lava with machines. What we can do is look for signs. Before an eruption, there are often a lot of small earthquakes, and the ground starts to rise. When we see these signs, we warn the villages.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What should young people study if they want your job?

turns.speaker: s
turns.text: Maths and physics, without question. I know they are not everybody’s favourite, but you need them to understand the data. Art and languages are interesting, but they won’t help you read what the machine says. So work hard at school, and don’t give up.

questions.prompt: Why did Andile become interested in volcanoes?
options: A family holiday took her to one
A video at school fascinated her
A book about lava excited her
questions.explanation: She never went near a volcano and did not read about lava; a video shown at school made her want to see it again.

questions.prompt: What does she do on some days?
options: Reads data from machines on the volcano
questions.explanation: She does not write stories or teach; she looks at numbers from machines on the volcano.

questions.prompt: How does she stay safe near a crater?
options: By wearing special masks and a helmet
By going only when it is cold
By carrying a lot of food and water
questions.explanation: She wears a helmet and a mask because of the gas; cold weather and food are not what keep her safe.

questions.prompt: How did she feel when she saw red lava at night?
questions.explanation: She says the prize was not it and she has met no famous scientist; the lava was so strong that she forgot to take pictures and smiled.

questions.prompt: What can scientists do before an eruption?
options: Name the exact day it will happen
See signs such as small earthquakes
Stop the lava with big machines
questions.explanation: They cannot give the exact date or stop lava; they look for small earthquakes and the ground rising.

questions.prompt: Why does she advise maths and physics?
options: They help to understand the data
questions.explanation: She knows they are not everybody’s favourite, but you need them to understand the data.

parts.title: Getting to know you

What do you do when there is a storm at home?
Have you ever visited a science museum?
Which natural wonder would you like to see?

parts.title: Describe a photograph
parts.instructions: Look at the photograph and speak for about one minute. Describe what you can see and say what the people might be feeling.
parts.prompt: A group of hikers looking at smoke coming from a volcano.

parts.title: Talk about the topic
parts.instructions: Answer the questions. Try to give a reason or an example with each answer.

questions.prompt: Why are natural disasters so frightening for people?
What should schools teach about safety in an emergency?
Would you like to be a scientist? Why or why not?
